title: Price It Like You Mean It

lessons.title: Anchor-based pricing, not cost-plus
body: Most beginners price by adding up the hours they spent making the product, their own hourly rate, production costs, and a margin on top. It feels fair — but it's misleading, because the customer paying you has no idea how many hours you spent, and wouldn't change their decision if they did. They care about the problem it solves, the outcome it helps them reach, and what else is available to solve the same problem. A price built from your hours answers a question the customer never asked.

Anchor-based pricing starts from the other side: a price anchor is a relevant reference point — what customers currently pay for a comparable product or an alternative way of solving the same problem — used to evaluate a proposed price, not generate one automatically. An anchor doesn't tell you what to charge. It tells you whether what you're about to charge is in a believable range for someone who already knows what alternatives cost.

Where to research comparable prices
1. Competitor websites and sales pages
Search for products solving the same problem, find their pricing pages, and note what's actually included — the promised outcome, and whether support, updates or bonuses come with it. Two products can share a price and mean very different things once you look past the number.
2. Digital product marketplaces
Gumroad, Etsy, Whop and similar marketplaces list guides, templates, toolkits, workbooks and courses at real, visible prices. Compare the actual product contents, not just the title — “content planner” can mean a single PDF or a full guided system.
3. Software and subscription alternatives
Some customers currently solve this problem with paid software. Check monthly and annual subscription costs, what the free plan leaves out, which features actually matter here, and — importantly — whether the software genuinely solves the same problem or just touches on it.
4. Freelancer and service alternatives
Sometimes the alternative is paying someone else directly — a designer, a virtual assistant, a consultant, a social media manager, a done-for-you service. Public rate sheets, published packages and marketplace listings give useful context, but a freelancer's price isn't automatically comparable to a self-service digital product — the customer is buying someone's time and judgment, not a one-time deliverable.
5. DIY and free alternatives
Free templates, free tutorials, YouTube videos, open-source tools and manual workarounds are real competition, even at $0 — they matter because they shape what your customer is already willing to accept without paying anything. A paid product isn't automatically more valuable than a free one; it has to earn the difference.

Search queries to try
Replace the brackets with your own niche, product category or outcome, and run several of these:
  • “[problem] template price”
  • “[niche] digital toolkit”
  • “[desired outcome] online course price”
  • “best [product category] alternatives”
  • “[service] freelance rates”
  • “[problem] software pricing”
  • “[product category] Gumroad” / “[product category] Etsy”
A hypothetical content creator pricing a social-media planning product might search “social media content planner price,” “content calendar Gumroad” and “social media manager freelance rates”; a hypothetical fitness coach pricing a workout program might instead search “beginner workout plan price,” “home workout program Etsy” and “personal trainer rates” — same method, different words.

Deciding what's actually comparable
Not every product in the same category is a useful anchor. Before using a price, compare the target audience, the problem being solved, the intended outcome, the product format, the depth of instruction, the number and usefulness of deliverables, the level of support, implementation difficulty, and how quickly the customer experiences value. A simple downloadable calendar template and a complete guided content-planning system both “relate to social media,” but comparing their prices directly would be misleading — one is a file, the other is a process.Sort each alternative you find into one of three categories:
  • Directly comparable — same problem, similar depth and format. Weigh this heavily.
  • Partially comparable — related problem or overlapping format, but a real gap in scope. Useful context, not a close anchor.
  • Alternative solution — solves the same underlying need through a different mechanism (software, a freelancer, doing it yourself). Shows what the customer is already willing to accept, but isn't a like-for-like price.

Keeping a price research log
Record what you find rather than trusting your memory of it. For each alternative, note: product or alternative name, source URL, price, currency, payment structure (one-time, monthly or annual), what's included, intended customer, main outcome, similarities to your offer, important differences, and which of the three comparison categories above it falls into. Collect several relevant alternatives where you can, rather than anchoring to just one. Never invent a competitor's price, listing or statistic you haven't actually seen — and remember that real prices change, so verify the current listing yourself before relying on it.A hypothetical content creator's research log for a social-media content planning product might look like this (illustrative numbers only — not real listings):
AlternativePriceCategory
A guided content-planning course covering the same weekly workflow$97 one-timeDirectly comparable
A marketplace listing selling only the design templates, no planning process$15 one-timePartially comparable
A social-media scheduling and analytics subscription tool$29/monthAlternative solution

Why this matters
Your hours are invisible to the customer and irrelevant to their decision. The alternatives they already know about are not — those are the real competition for their money, whether or not you ever look at them. Anchoring to what they can already see keeps your price inside the range of things they'll actually consider, instead of a number that only makes sense from your side of the transaction.
lessons.insight: Price your product against the alternatives your customer considers, not just the hours you spent creating it.

lessons.title: Set your price
body: With your research log from Lesson 6.1 in hand, review it before proposing anything: remove comparisons that turned out irrelevant, identify the closest alternatives, understand what customers actually pay for them, compare their deliverables and outcome against your own offer, and note where your product sits relative to each one. One unusually expensive or unusually cheap listing shouldn't decide your whole price — where you have several relevant alternatives, use the range they form rather than fixating on a single number, and don't treat an average or median as meaningful if the underlying products aren't genuinely comparable to begin with.

How offer strength affects price
Your anchor tells you the believable range; what you actually build tells you where in that range you can credibly sit. Four things from Module 3 shape the customer's assessment: how valuable and desirable the outcome is, how much confidence they have that it'll work, how quickly they can expect to experience value, and how much effort it asks of them. Alongside those, the depth of your core deliverable, the relevance of your bonuses, the quality of your implementation guidance, the support and access you offer, and the overall completeness of the product all factor in. None of this means more bonuses automatically justifies a higher price — a product with five loosely-related extras isn't worth more than one with two that genuinely matter. The price has to make sense against the real customer experience and the real alternatives, not against how much is technically included.

What your Pull/Drag position tells you
A Magnetic offer — strong, credible, low resistance — generally has more room to price closer to a relevant comparable alternative than a weaker offer still carrying real resistance. A Slow Burn offer, wanted but still resisted, usually needs more improvement before it can support a similar price to a stronger competitor. But treat this as a direction to lean, not a formula: the Pull/Drag Map is a diagnostic tool, not a pricing calculator. Don't build an automatic multiplier off your M3 scores, and don't assume landing in any particular zone guarantees customers will pay a specific amount — it only tells you roughly how much room you currently have to work with.

Choosing a starting price
  1. Review your closest price anchors from Lesson 6.1.
  2. Review your unique value proposition from Module 5, and how strongly it supports standing apart from the anchor.
  3. Compare the scope and completeness of your offer against them.
  4. Consider how much uncertainty still remains — for the customer, and for you.
  5. Consider the level of support and implementation effort you're providing.
  6. Identify a plausible initial price.
  7. Explain the reasoning behind it, in writing, so you can revisit it later.
  8. Record what still needs to be validated before you'd trust this number.
Keep four different things separate in your head, because beginners routinely merge them into one: a price you personally prefer, a price competitors happen to charge, a price customers might realistically accept, and a price you've actually validated with real buyers. Only the last one is proven — everything before Module 8 is still a reasoned guess, however well-researched.

Continuing the worked example — hypothetical
Back to the hypothetical content creator from Lesson 6.1. Of the three alternatives logged, the $97 guided course is the closest anchor — same weekly workflow, similar depth. The $15 template-only listing is partially comparable (it covers design, not planning), and the $29/month scheduling tool is a different payment structure entirely, so it's noted as context rather than compared directly. On the Pull/Drag Map from Module 3, this offer scored Outcome Pull 8, Proof Pull 4, Speed Drag 6, Effort Drag 7 — landing in Slow Burn, not Magnetic: real interest, but real resistance too, mainly from weak Proof Pull. That's a reason to price meaningfully below the $97 anchor rather than at or above it, at least until that resistance is addressed. A plausible starting price here is $47 — above the templates-only product, since this includes a full planning system plus three bonuses, but well below the closest full course, reflecting that trust in this specific offer hasn't been established yet. What still needs validating: whether $47 actually feels fair to someone who's never bought from this creator before, and whether the bonuses are pulling their weight at that price.

The discount-to-anchor calculation
The exercise below calculates how far your proposed price sits below your anchor: (Anchor price − Proposed price) ÷ Anchor price × 100. For example, a comparable anchor of $50 against a proposed price of $35 is a $15 difference — a 30% discount relative to the anchor. Applied to the worked example above, a $97 anchor against a $47 price is a $50 difference, roughly a 52% discount. This is simply arithmetic, not a judgment — it doesn't prove your price is attractive, fair or optimal, and there's no universal discount range this lesson will hand you as a rule. If you do develop a hypothesis about what discount range feels right for your situation, treat it as exactly that — a hypothesis to weigh against product differences, customer expectations and real buying behaviour, not a target to hit. Comparing across different currencies or between one-time and recurring pricing also needs care — a $29/month tool isn't directly comparable to a $47 one-time purchase without thinking through what a customer would actually pay over time.

The same method, a different niche — hypothetical
A hypothetical fitness coach pricing a beginner home-workout program might find a closest anchor of $79 for a comparable 4-week program elsewhere, note that personal training sessions run $40–$60 each as a (less comparable) alternative solution, and — if their own Pull/Drag position is closer to Magnetic than Slow Burn — reasonably price nearer to that $79 anchor than our content creator did. Same method, different starting point, different answer — which is the point.

A reasoned position, not a formula
Nothing in this lesson adds up to a single correct number — the anchor, your offer's strength, and your Pull/Drag position all narrow the range and inform the reasoning, but none of them calculate the price for you. The goal is a number you chose for stated reasons, not one you can prove in advance.
lessons.insight: A starting price is a reasoned position, not a formula — your research and your offer's strength narrow the range, but neither one calculates the number for you.

lessons.title: Understand your pricing decision
body:
Before moving on, run your proposed price through a short checklist:
  • Is the anchor genuinely relevant, or just the first thing I found?
  • Have I compared enough alternatives to actually understand this market?
  • Am I comparing similar deliverables, not just a similar topic?
  • Does my product solve a meaningful problem?
  • Can I explain, in plain language, why my offer costs what it does?
  • Does the price reflect the actual depth and usefulness of the product?
  • Is this realistic for the customer I'm actually targeting?
  • Have I confused what competitors charge with what customers have proven they'll pay?
If you can answer all eight honestly, you have a defensible starting hypothesis — not a proven price, but a reasonable one to test.

Common pricing mistakes
  1. Pricing entirely on personal effort. Go back to Lesson 6.1 and anchor against alternatives instead.
  2. Copying a competitor's price without understanding their offer. Check depth, support and format before matching a number.
  3. Choosing the cheapest price out of fear. A price that's too low to be credible can hurt trust as much as one that's too high.
  4. Charging more simply because the product has many bonuses. Bonuses support the core; they don't multiply the price on their own.
  5. Using an irrelevant premium product as an anchor. Re-check it against the “directly / partially / alternative” test from Lesson 6.1.
  6. Assuming social media engagement proves willingness to pay. Likes and comments aren't purchases — Module 8 is where that actually gets tested.
  7. Treating the discount calculation as validation. It's arithmetic against your own anchor, not evidence that anyone will buy.
  8. Changing the price repeatedly without collecting real evidence. Pick a documented hypothesis and test it, rather than guessing again every few days.

Preparing to test this price
Everything in this module produces a hypothesis, not a verified fact — you still have to find out whether real people will actually pay this amount. It helps to keep these four reactions distinct, because beginners often treat the first as proof and it isn't: someone saying the price sounds reasonable, someone expressing interest, someone taking a real step toward buying, and someone actually paying. Only the last two carry real weight. Module 8 covers how to test that properly — this lesson's job is only to make sure you're carrying a clearly documented price and reasoning into that test, not a vague feeling about what “seems about right.”

Why a documented hypothesis beats endless guessing
A price you arrived at through research, that you can explain in two sentences, is something you can actually test and learn from. A number you agonised over without writing down why just leaves you guessing again later, with nothing to learn from either way. Being wrong here costs nothing — the whole point of Module 8 is finding out, cheaply, before it matters.

Closing the worked example — hypothetical
The hypothetical content creator from Lessons 6.1 and 6.2 now carries a documented $47 starting price, anchored against a $97 comparable course, reasoned from a Slow Burn Pull/Drag position with weak Proof Pull. Into Module 8, two assumptions still need testing: whether $47 feels fair to someone who has never bought from this creator before, and whether the three bonuses are actually pulling their weight at that price rather than just padding it. Neither assumption gets resolved by thinking about it harder — only by asking real people.
lessons.insight: Your price is a hypothesis to test in Module 8, not a final decision — it's fine to be wrong here.

exercise.instructions: Enter what the closest existing alternative costs, then set your price. The discount-to-anchor percentage is a sanity check, not a recommendation.

prompt.title: Pricing Prompt
prompt.purpose: Use this to pressure-test your price against a real anchor.
prompt.template: You are a pricing consultant for a new digital/service offer. My offer stack: {{m4.summary}}. What customers currently pay for the closest existing alternative, my anchor: {{m6.anchorPrice}}. My proposed price: {{m6.price}}. Review my proposed price against the anchor and my offer stack — tell me whether it's justified relative to the anchor, not based on my time or costs, and explain your reasoning in two sentences. If I haven't given you a real anchor price or proposed price, tell me what's missing and ask for it before reviewing anything. If my anchor price looks like it's for a meaningfully different — bigger or smaller — thing than what I'm actually offering, point that out before using it. Flag anything in my price or reasoning that rests on an assumption rather than something I've actually told you. Name one specific thing about this price that still needs to be validated with real customers in Module 8. Return: whether my proposed price holds up, one sentence of reasoning, and one sentence naming the main risk of pricing it this way. Don't cite pricing-psychology statistics or market data you don't actually have — reason only from the anchor and stack I've given you.
